[1, 2] The proclamation authorizes the use of all available state and local government resources to address the ongoing drought. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A July 25, 2024, report from the U.S. Drought Monitor confirmed that after being declared drought-free on June 11, 2024, Ohio and Kentucky experienced a rapid expansion of drought conditions. [4] The primary causes for the deterioration were extreme heat and below-normal rainfall over the preceding five weeks. [4] The report, which uses data valid through July 23, 2024, indicated a significant expansion of "abnormally dry" (D0) and "moderate drought" (D1) classifications across the eastern Corn Belt. [4, 7] Impacts noted in both states included below-normal soil moisture stressing crops, fair to poor pasture conditions, and below-normal streamflows. [4] <2> On July 23, 2024, the U.S. Drought Monitor reported that 17.0% of the United States and Puerto Rico were under moderate to exceptional drought conditions. [1] Improvements, with a reduction in drought or abnormal dryness, were noted in parts of the Southwest, the southern Plains, the Lower Mississippi Valley to the Southeast, and the Mid-Atlantic coast. [1] Conversely, persistent dryness and heat led to the expansion or intensification of drought across much of Hawaii, as well as parts of the West, the central to northern Plains, and a region stretching from the Ohio Valley to the mid-Appalachians. [1] <3> A study by researchers at the University of Alabama, published in the journal Environmental Research Letters, found that droughts cost the U.S. hydropower industry an estimated $28 billion between 2003 and 2020. The losses stemmed from a reduction of about 300 million megawatt-hours of electricity generation, highlighting the sector's vulnerability to drought conditions. The study noted that to compensate for the hydropower deficit, utilities relied more on natural gas, which led to a 10% increase in carbon dioxide emissions over the 18-year period. California, Washington, and Oregon were the most affected states, accounting for half of the drop in power generation. The estimated economic losses were over $8.7 billion in California, $4.2 billion in Washington, and $1.6 billion in Oregon. <4> A weekly report from the U.S. Drought Monitor, published on July 18, 2024, indicated that as of July 16, 2024, moderate to exceptional drought covered 17.4% of the United States and Puerto Rico. [2] This marked an increase from the previous week's 16.4%. [2] The report noted that continued dryness and heat caused drought conditions to expand or intensify across much of the West, the Deep South to the central Appalachians, as well as parts of the Plains and Hawaii. [2] <5> A U.S. Drought Monitor report released on July 11, 2024, stated that as of July 9, 2024, moderate to exceptional drought covered 16.4% of the United States including Puerto Rico. This marked an increase from the 15.8% recorded in the prior week. The report noted that continued heat and dryness led to the expansion or intensification of drought conditions in the Pacific Northwest, extending to the northern High Plains, across sections of the southern Plains, and from the Southeast to the Mid-Atlantic states. <6> On July 10, 2024, a special drought status update was issued for Pacific Northwest Tribal Nations, addressing the impacts of developing drought conditions. The report, a collaboration involving the National Integrated Drought Information System (NIDIS), highlighted that a below-normal snowpack, early snowmelt, and recent dryness were leading to declining streamflows. At the time of the report, nearly half of the tribal lands in the region were classified as abnormally dry, with an additional 29.2% in a state of moderate to severe drought. The Coeur d'Alene Reservation, in particular, had approximately 23% of its area experiencing severe drought. Forecasts predicted above-normal temperatures and below-normal precipitation through September, which was expected to worsen drought conditions and increase wildland fire potential. The update also warned of significant impacts, including potential hardships for livestock and agriculture, and projected that some river flows could decline to levels that would strand migrating fish, threatening critical species. [2, 7] These regulations do not directly penalize individual or business water use but instead set customized water-use objectives for each supplier based on local factors like climate, population, and land use. [2, 3] While the rules are effective in 2025, enforcement, including potential fines of up to $10,000 per day for non-compliant suppliers, will not begin until 2027. [2, 5] The phased cutbacks are scheduled for 2027, 2030, 2035, and 2040, with the ultimate goal of achieving a cumulative savings of 500,000-acre feet of water annually by 2040. [5] This move was prompted by legislation signed in 2018 to create a long-term framework for water conservation, shifting from reactive, temporary restrictions during droughts to a proactive approach to ensure future water resilience. [2, 6] The required reductions vary significantly by water supplier; for instance, some in the Bay Area will see minimal cuts, while others, like the Desert Water Agency, face reductions as high as 32% by 2040. In North Carolina, the significant rainfall in July allowed armyworms to spread largely undetected. <9> The U.S. climate outlook for July 2024, issued by NOAA's Climate Prediction Center, predicted widespread drought development across large portions of the northwestern, south-central, and eastern parts of the country. This forecast was based on the expectation of above-normal temperatures across nearly the entire nation and below-normal rainfall in many of these same areas. The outlook, released at the end of June, noted that nearly 30% of the nation was already abnormally dry, and worsening soil moisture conditions during June set the stage for the anticipated drought. Specifically, the forecast favored well-above-average temperatures for almost the entire contiguous U.S. and well-below-average precipitation in a region stretching from the Pacific Northwest to the Southern Plains. <10> According to the U.S. Drought Monitor report from June 25, 2024, moderate to exceptional drought extended across 13.6% of the United States and Puerto Rico. This represented a significant increase from the 10.1% reported in the preceding week. The expansion and intensification of drought conditions were attributed to a combination of high temperatures and sustained dry weather. These deteriorating conditions were most pronounced across large areas of the Southeast, the Mid-Atlantic states, and the Ohio Valley. Additionally, drought or abnormal dryness also worsened in the Pacific Northwest and the northern Rockies.

metadata.original_text: This time series records drought data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2024-12-22 to 2025-03-09. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, as of December 10, 2024, nearly the entire Northeast region was affected by dryness and drought conditions. Extreme Drought (D3) was ongoing in Massachusetts, while Severe Drought (D2) persisted across most of southern New England, southeast New York, and Long Island. However, recent widespread rainfall and lake effect snow events had started to alleviate the situation, improving conditions by benefiting surface soils and streamflows where the ground was not frozen, and significantly reducing the risk of fire. <2> On December 11, 2024, a report was issued indicating the development of snow drought conditions across the northern Rocky Mountains. The report highlighted that substantial snow water equivalent (SWE) deficits had emerged in areas, including Wyoming and southwestern Montana, where many SNOTEL stations were reporting SWE below the 10th percentile, with some at record lows for the date. These conditions were attributed to a combination of above-average temperatures and low precipitation, which had persisted into the new water year. The report noted that a poor start to the water year could lead to expanded drought conditions, increased wildfire risk, and low river levels. <3> According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, as of December 3, 2024, moderate to exceptional drought covered 36.5% of the United States, including Puerto Rico. This marked an increase from the previous week's figure of 34.7%. Drought conditions were reported to have expanded or intensified in several areas, including parts of Hawaii, the Rockies, the Lower Mississippi and Tennessee Valleys, as well as in the Carolinas, Virginia, and northern regions of the Northeast. <4> In late 2024, drought conditions led to historically low water levels in both the Mississippi and Delaware Rivers, causing significant saltwater intrusion that threatened municipal and industrial water supplies. For the third consecutive year, a saltwater wedge from the Gulf of Mexico crept up the Mississippi River, a phenomenon occurring when river flow drops below 300,000 cubic feet per second. This created a public health crisis in southeast Louisiana, particularly in Plaquemines Parish, where residents were forced to use bottled water as the saltwater contaminated drinking sources. Similarly, a rainless start to the fall in the U.S. Northeast caused the salt front on the Delaware River to move approximately 17 to 20 miles north of its usual location to the vicinity of Philadelphia International Airport. This event prompted officials to release fresh water from upstream reservoirs to push the salt line back downstream and protect the drinking water for about 14 million people in Philadelphia and surrounding areas in New Jersey and New York. While drinking water was not imminently at risk, the salt front was the closest it had been to the city's primary water intakes in eight years, raising concerns about future water security amid rising sea levels and more frequent droughts. <5> In November 2024, unusually dry conditions combined with warmth, low humidity, and strong winds led to a record number of Red Flag Warnings for fire weather risk across the Northeast, an atypical situation for a time of year when fire risk is normally low. The National Weather Service issued a high number of warnings, setting new records in several states since 2006. Connecticut and Massachusetts recorded the most warnings for any month of the year, while Rhode Island tied its all-time monthly record. Furthermore, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Vermont, New Hampshire, and West Virginia set records for the most warnings in any November, with Maryland and Delaware tying their respective November records. This heightened fire risk is abnormal for the region, where the peak season is typically March through May. <6> On November 5, 2024, data revealed a widespread drought across the United States, with 49 states experiencing some level of drought. A record 87.8% of the contiguous 48 states was reported as being at least abnormally dry. Within this area, pockets of extreme drought (D3) were confirmed in portions of New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, West Virginia, Tennessee, Alabama, and Mississippi. This information was published on November 7, 2024. <7> In its November 2024 Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) projected that electricity generation from U.S. hydropower plants in 2024 would be 13% below the 10-year average, marking the lowest output since 2001. [2] The forecast attributed the decline to widespread extreme and exceptional drought conditions, particularly in the Pacific Northwest, a region that hosts the majority of U.S. hydropower capacity. [2] This forecast was a significant reversal from an April 2024 projection, which had anticipated a 6% increase in hydropower generation for the year. [1, 2] <8> The National Weather Service (NWS) in Goodland, Kansas, issued a Drought Information Statement on November 4, 2024, confirming that drought conditions had worsened across the Tri-State area. The report stated that most of the plains received well-below-normal precipitation during October, contributing to the deteriorating conditions. Specifically, the NWS identified worsening drought in Colorado's Yuma and Kit Carson counties; Nebraska's Dundy, Hitchcock, and Red Willow counties; and Kansas' Cheyenne, Sherman, Wallace, Thomas, Logan, Gove, Greeley, Decatur, Norton, and Wichita counties. An exception was noted for Cheyenne County, Colorado, where drought conditions had improved. <9> On November 2, 2024, New York City Mayor Eric Adams and the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) Commissioner Rohit T. Aggarwala issued a citywide drought watch. [3, 7] This action was taken in response to a historic lack of precipitation, with October 2024 being the driest October in the city's recorded history and marking its second-longest dry streak. [3, 7] As part of the drought watch, the first of three levels of water conservation declarations, Mayor Adams ordered all city agencies to update their water conservation plans and prepare for implementation. [3, 9] The public was strongly urged to conserve water through measures such as taking shorter showers, not letting taps run while brushing teeth, and reporting open fire hydrants to 311. [9, 10] On the same day, the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation also declared a drought watch for 15 counties, including the five boroughs of New York City. [6, 11] The city later elevated the declaration to a 'drought warning' on November 18, 2024. [5] <10> A record-breaking flash drought intensified across the United States in October 2024, driven by a persistent and strong ridge of high pressure that led to unusually warm and dry conditions. By October 29, 2024, a state of abnormal dryness and drought impacted over 78% of the American population. This marked the highest percentage of the population affected by drought in the 25-year history of the U.S. Drought Monitor. The severity of the conditions was further evidenced by over 70 weather stations across the country recording their driest October ever.

This situation, which has also affected the Ohio River's contribution to the Mississippi's flow, forces grain shippers to lighten barge loads during the peak season for transporting Midwest corn and soybeans for export.
